blurb: Everyday eats: where they started and how they got their names

questions.q: The hamburger takes its name from which German city?
questions.fact: Before 'hamburger' caught on, American menus called the dish a 'Hamburg steak.'
questions.src: etymonline hamburger: meat sense 'so called by 1880 (as hamburg steak)', sandwich 1909

questions.q: A jalapeno that has been smoked and dried goes by what name?
questions.fact: The jalapeno itself is named after Xalapa, the capital of the Mexican state of Veracruz.
questions.src: Recipes wiki jalapeno page: named after Jalapa, capital of Veracruz; smoked dried = chipotle

questions.q: Tangerines are named after Tangier, a port city in which country?
questions.fact: The name took hold in the 1800s, when the fruit was shipped to Britain from Tangier.
questions.src: etymonline tangerine: from Tangier, Morocco; noun 1842, originally imported to Britain from there

questions.q: Salisbury steak is named after James Salisbury, a 19th-century American who worked as what?
questions.fact: Dr. J.H. Salisbury promoted the dish, and the name 'Salisbury steak' shows up in print by 1885.
questions.src: etymonline Salisbury: J.H. Salisbury (1823-1905), US physician, attested 1885

questions.q: The potato was first farmed thousands of years ago in which mountain range?
questions.fact: Farmers near Lake Titicaca, on the modern Peru-Bolivia border, grew potatoes 7,000 to 10,000 years ago.
questions.src: Wikipedia Potato: domesticated southern Peru / NW Bolivia near Lake Titicaca

questions.q: Sam Panopoulos, widely credited with inventing Hawaiian pizza, ran his restaurant in which country?
questions.fact: He said he named it after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
questions.src: Canadian Encyclopedia 'Hawaiian pizza': Panopoulos, Satellite Restaurant, Chatham, Ontario (opened 1962); named after canned pineapple brand; competing claims noted, so 1962 invention date dropped

questions.q: The kiwifruit is native to which country?
questions.fact: It was sold as the 'Chinese gooseberry' until a New Zealand exporter renamed it in 1959.
questions.src: Wikipedia Kiwifruit: native to central/eastern China; renamed 1959 by Turners & Growers

questions.q: Archaeologists found signs of banana farming about 6,800 years old at Kuk Swamp, in which country?
questions.fact: UNESCO added Kuk to its World Heritage List in 2008 as an early farming site.
questions.src: Sapiens.org banana domestication (~6,800 yrs); UNESCO WHC list/887: inscribed 2008, agriculture 7,000-6,400 years ago based on bananas, taro, yam

questions.q: Swanson's first TV dinner, in 1953, centered on which holiday-style main course?
questions.fact: It sold for 98 cents in a three-compartment aluminum tray, in a box styled to look like a TV set.
questions.src: National Geographic + History.com: turkey, cornbread stuffing, peas, sweet potatoes; 98 cents

questions.q: In 1789, a mold for making macaroni was bought in Naples for which future president?
questions.fact: Jefferson later ordered pasta from Europe, and a macaroni and cheese recipe in his handwriting survives.
questions.src: Monticello.org 'Macaroni': William Short procured a 'mould for making maccaroni' in Naples, Feb 1789; Jefferson regularly ordered pasta from Europe; mac-and-cheese recipe in his hand. Replaced '1802 state dinner' Q (Monticello: Cutler's 'pie called macaroni', not documented as mac and cheese or a state dinner; machine not brought home by TJ)

questions.q: Goldfish crackers were invented in 1958 in which country, before Pepperidge Farm sold them in the US?
questions.fact: Swiss biscuit maker Oscar Kambly created them; Pepperidge Farm launched them in America in 1962.
questions.src: Wikipedia Goldfish (cracker): Kambly, Switzerland, 1958; US 1962

questions.q: Sriracha sauce is named after Si Racha, a seaside town in which country?
questions.fact: Huy Fong Foods is named after the ship that carried founder David Tran's family to Hong Kong.
questions.src: Britannica sriracha: named for Si Racha; Huy Fong named for the Taiwanese ship that delivered Tran and family to Hong Kong

blurb: Halloween dress-up, candy bags and pumpkin patch history

questions.q: A red-and-white striped shirt, bobble hat and round glasses make a costume of which character?
questions.fact: He debuted in Britain in 1987 as Wally; his American publisher renamed him Waldo.
questions.src: Wikipedia Where's Wally?: Martin Handford, 1987, UK; renamed Waldo in North America

questions.q: Jenna Ortega starred as which famously gloomy character in a 2022 Netflix series?
questions.fact: Lisa Loring played the role in the 1964 TV series, and Christina Ricci in the 1991 film.
questions.src: Wikipedia Wednesday Addams

questions.q: In L. Frank Baum's 1900 book, what color were Dorothy's magic shoes?
questions.fact: The 1939 film made them ruby to show off its three-strip Technicolor process.
questions.src: Wikipedia Ruby slippers: Silver Shoes in novel; changed for Technicolor

questions.q: The Addams Family began in 1938 as single-panel cartoons in which magazine?
questions.fact: The live-action TV series premiered on ABC in September 1964 and ran for two seasons.
questions.src: Wikipedia The Addams Family: first cartoon 1938 in The New Yorker; ABC Sept 18, 1964

questions.q: Classic candy corn has three stripes: white, orange and what color?
questions.fact: Candy corn dates to the 1880s, and it was once sold under the name 'Chicken Feed.'
questions.src: Wikipedia Candy corn + Daily Meal: 1880s, Renninger/Wunderle; 'Chicken Feed'; yellow/orange/white

questions.q: H.B. Reese, maker of Reese's Peanut Butter Cups, once worked for which chocolate maker?
questions.fact: His peanut butter cups date to 1928, and his sons merged the company with Hershey in 1963.
questions.src: Wikipedia Reese's Peanut Butter Cups: created Nov 15, 1928; Reese former dairy farmer and shipping foreman for Milton S. Hershey; merged with Hershey July 2, 1963. Candy Hall of Fame confirms. 'Creator of the peanut butter cup' dropped (truetreats: he did not invent the PB cup)

questions.q: When 3 Musketeers debuted in 1932, it came in three pieces: chocolate, vanilla and what flavor?
questions.fact: Rising costs and wartime sugar limits led Mars to drop the vanilla and strawberry pieces.
questions.src: Wikipedia 3 Musketeers: 1932, three flavors chocolate/strawberry/vanilla; vanilla and strawberry phased out due to rising costs and wartime sugar restrictions

questions.q: Kit Kat was launched in England in 1935 under what original name?
questions.fact: Rowntree's had trademarked the names Kit Cat and Kit Kat back in 1911.
questions.src: Wikipedia KitKat: launched Sept 1935 as Rowntree's Chocolate Crisp; Rowntree's trademarked 'Kit Cat' and 'Kit Kat' in 1911. Old fact (name came from Kit-Cat Club) not stated as established, replaced

questions.q: In 'It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown,' who waits all night in the pumpkin patch?
questions.fact: The special first aired in 1966, and Charlie Brown's trick-or-treat bag famously fills with rocks.
questions.src: Wikipedia It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown: CBS Oct 27, 1966 (CBC Oct 26); Linus holds vigil; Charlie Brown only gets rocks

questions.q: Before pumpkins, people in Ireland and Scotland carved Halloween lanterns from which vegetable?
questions.fact: Before it meant a carved lantern, 'jack-o'-lantern' was a name for the will-o'-the-wisp, an eerie marsh light.
questions.src: Wikipedia Jack-o'-lantern: turnips and mangel wurzels hollowed out as lanterns in Ireland, Scotland, etc.; etymonline: name for the ignis fatuus by 1650s, carved pumpkin sense by 1828

questions.q: Pumpkins belong to the same plant family as which of these?
questions.fact: The gourd family also includes watermelons, zucchini and cantaloupes.
questions.src: Textbook botany: Cucurbitaceae

questions.q: Which author's 1697 Cinderella, with a fairy godmother and a pumpkin coach, became the classic version?
questions.fact: In the Brothers Grimm version, published in 1812, a magic hazel tree and birds help her instead.
questions.src: Textbook literature: Perrault's Cendrillon 1697; Grimm Aschenputtel 1812

blurb: Halloween customs worldwide, monster classics and trick-or-treat roots

questions.q: Who wrote the 1897 vampire novel Dracula?
questions.fact: Stoker was Irish and spent years as business manager of London's Lyceum Theatre.
questions.src: Textbook literature

questions.q: Which author wrote the Goosebumps book series for kids?
questions.fact: The first Goosebumps book, Welcome to Dead House, came out in 1992.
questions.src: Textbook (Scholastic, 1992)

questions.q: In Mary Shelley's novel, what is the first name of the scientist Frankenstein?
questions.fact: Shelley began the story at 18, during a ghost-story challenge near Lake Geneva in 1816.
questions.src: Textbook literature (Villa Diodati, summer 1816; novel 1818)

questions.q: Who wrote the 1886 novella Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde?
questions.fact: Stevenson had already published Treasure Island as a book in 1883.
questions.src: Textbook literature

questions.q: The name Halloween comes from 'All Hallows' Eve,' the evening before which day?
questions.fact: 'Hallow' is an old word for saint, so All Hallows' Day is another name for All Saints' Day.
questions.src: Textbook etymology

questions.q: Starting in 1950, trick-or-treaters began collecting coins for which children's aid group?
questions.fact: UNICEF itself was founded in 1946 to help children after World War II.
questions.src: SOFII case study: Trick-or-Treat for UNICEF began 1950 with a Philadelphia class collecting coins; UNICEF founded 1946 textbook

questions.q: In Scotland and Ireland, going door to door in costume at Halloween is traditionally called what?
questions.fact: Guisers were traditionally expected to sing a song, tell a joke or share a story to earn their treat.
questions.src: National Records of Scotland blog 'Out guising': guisers tour houses in costume and must perform (jokes, songs) for a reward. 'First-footing' distractor swapped for 'Dooking' (it is the answer key in the Countdown deck)

questions.q: Small spiced cakes given to door-to-door visitors around Hallowmas in medieval England were called what?
questions.fact: This custom, called souling, is often cited as one root of trick-or-treating.
questions.src: Wikipedia Soul cake: small round cake with sweet spices, given to soulers door to door at Allhallowtide; practice dates to medieval period in England; souling seen as an origin of trick-or-treating

questions.q: Which 2017 Pixar film is set during Mexico's Day of the Dead?
questions.fact: Day of the Dead is celebrated on November 1 and 2, right after Halloween.
questions.src: Textbook

questions.q: Halloween traces its roots to which ancient Celtic festival?
questions.fact: Samhain marked the end of the harvest season and the start of winter.
questions.src: Textbook

questions.q: In Ireland, which fruit-studded bread is a Halloween tradition, often with a ring baked inside?
questions.fact: 'Brack' comes from the Irish word breac, meaning speckled, a nod to the dried fruit.
questions.src: Textbook (bairin breac)

questions.q: Day of the Dead altars are decked with orange flowers called cempasuchil. What flower is it?
questions.fact: Its name comes from the Aztecs' Nahuatl language and is often translated as 'twenty flower.'
questions.src: Textbook (Tagetes erecta, Mexican marigold)

blurb: A world tour of famous dishes and the places they call home

questions.q: Paella, the saffron rice dish cooked in a wide pan, comes from which country?
questions.fact: Paella is a Valencian word meaning frying pan, named for the shallow pan it's cooked in.
questions.src: Wikipedia Paella: from Valencian Community; 'Paella is a Valencian word that means frying pan'

questions.q: Poutine, fries topped with cheese curds and gravy, comes from which Canadian province?
questions.fact: Poutine first appeared in rural Quebec snack bars in the late 1950s.
questions.src: Canadian Encyclopedia 'History of poutine': rural Quebec snack bars, late 1950s

questions.q: Beef Stroganoff is named after a noble family from which country?
questions.fact: The earliest known recipe appears in an 1871 Russian cookbook by Elena Molokhovets.
questions.src: Wikipedia Beef Stroganoff: Stroganov family, Russia; Molokhovets 1871 edition

questions.q: Bobotie, spiced minced meat baked under an egg topping, is a classic dish of which country?
questions.fact: The egg-based topping bakes into a golden, custard-like layer over the spiced meat.
questions.src: Wikipedia Bobotie: 'a South African dish consisting of spiced minced meat baked with an egg-based topping'

questions.q: Jerk chicken, seasoned with allspice and Scotch bonnet peppers, comes from which island?
questions.fact: In Jamaica, allspice is called pimento, not to be confused with the red pepper in olives.
questions.src: Tasting Table history of jerk: Scotch bonnet, pimento = local name for allspice

questions.q: Vietnam's banh mi sandwich is served on a baguette, a legacy of which country?
questions.fact: Banh mi simply means 'bread' in Vietnamese.
questions.src: Wikipedia Banh mi: means bread; French introduced the baguette during colonial rule

questions.q: In Egypt, falafel is usually made from which bean instead of chickpeas?
questions.fact: Egyptians call their fava bean version ta'ameya.
questions.src: Wikipedia Falafel: 'In Egypt, it is typically prepared with fava beans'; called ta'miyya

questions.q: Osaka's takoyaki are savory batter balls filled with pieces of what?
questions.fact: A street vendor named Tomekichi Endo is credited with inventing takoyaki in 1935.
questions.src: Wikipedia Takoyaki: filled with octopus; Tomekichi Endo 1935; popularized in Osaka

questions.q: The French word croissant means what?
questions.fact: Its shape came from the Austrian kipferl, sold in Paris by a Viennese bakery in the late 1830s.
questions.src: Wikipedia Croissant: 'crescent'; kipferl; August Zang's Boulangerie Viennoise 1838/1839

questions.q: The cheese dish fondue gets its name from a French word meaning what?
questions.fact: Fondue's popularity in the United States peaked in the 1960s and 1970s.
questions.src: Wikipedia Fondue: from fondre 'to melt', means 'melted'; US popularity peaked 1960s-70s

questions.q: In Arabic, the word hummus means what?
questions.fact: The dip's full Arabic name translates to 'chickpeas with tahini.'
questions.src: Wikipedia Hummus: hummus = chickpeas; full name hummus bi tahina 'chickpeas with tahini'

questions.q: In Italian, the pasta name spaghetti means what?
questions.fact: Linguine means 'little tongues,' and vermicelli means 'little worms.'
questions.src: etymologynerd.com 'little cords': spaghetti = little strings/cords from spago; linguine = little tongues; vermicelli/orecchiette textbook

blurb: Apples, squash, cranberries and the rest of fall's harvest

questions.q: The Fuji apple was developed in which country?
questions.fact: Japanese researchers made the cross in 1939, but the Fuji wasn't named and released until 1962.
questions.src: Wikipedia Fuji (apple): developed 1939, Tohoku Research Station, Fujisaki; named and brought to market 1962. applesandpeople.org.uk confirms 1939 cross / 1962 registration. Old fact 'named for Fujisaki' dropped: sources disagree (Mt. Fuji also cited)

questions.q: What was the real name of the American folk hero Johnny Appleseed?
questions.fact: Born in Massachusetts in 1774, he planted tree nurseries rather than orchards.
questions.src: Wikipedia Johnny Appleseed: John Chapman, b. Sept 26, 1774, Leominster MA; 'planted nurseries rather than orchards'

questions.q: The tart green Granny Smith apple originated in which country?
questions.fact: It began in 1868 near Sydney, discovered by an orchardist named Maria Ann Smith.
questions.src: Wikipedia Granny Smith: Eastwood NSW (Sydney suburb), 1868, Maria Ann Smith

questions.q: The Honeycrisp apple, released in 1991, was developed at which university?
questions.fact: Washington State University crossed Honeycrisp with Enterprise to create the Cosmic Crisp, launched in 2019.
questions.src: America's Test Kitchen: U of Minnesota released Honeycrisp 1991; WSU Cosmic Crisp = Honeycrisp x Enterprise, Oct 2019

questions.q: Which winter squash's cooked flesh pulls apart into long, noodle-like strands?
questions.fact: Butternut, acorn and spaghetti squash are all winter squash, picked once their rinds turn hard.
questions.src: Univ. of Illinois Extension: butternut, acorn, spaghetti are winter squash; harvest when rind is hard and can't be punctured with a fingernail

questions.q: Corn, beans and squash planted together are traditionally known as the Three what?
questions.fact: Squash's broad leaves shade the soil, keeping it moist and crowding out weeds.
questions.src: Wikipedia Three Sisters (agriculture): squash leaves shade ground, retain moisture, limit weeds

questions.q: Squash was first domesticated on which continent?
questions.fact: Squash was grown in Oaxaca, Mexico, about 10,000 years ago, one of the oldest crops of the Americas.
questions.src: FAO AGRIS record: C. pepo cultivation at Guila Naquitz, Oaxaca, 10,000-8,000 years ago

questions.q: The English word squash was borrowed from the language of which Native American people?
questions.fact: The original word, askutasquash, meant roughly 'the things that may be eaten raw.'
questions.src: etymonline squash (n.2): 1640s, from Narragansett askutasquash 'the things that may be eaten raw'

questions.q: Cranberries grow on low vines in sandy wetlands known as what?
questions.fact: Wild cranberries are native to North America.
questions.src: Popular Science 'Cranberries can bounce, float': grown in bogs; wild cranberries native to North America

questions.q: Why do cranberries float when growers flood the fields at harvest?
questions.fact: Each berry holds four air pockets, which is also why fresh cranberries bounce.
questions.src: Popular Science: each cranberry contains four air pockets; bounce test for freshness

questions.q: The orange 'yams' sold in most US grocery stores are actually what?
questions.fact: True yams belong to a different plant family and are native to Africa and Asia.
questions.src: HuffPost 2013 sweet potatoes vs yams: orange 'yams' are sweet potatoes; true yams Dioscoreaceae, Africa/Asia

questions.q: Apples, pears, cherries and strawberries all belong to which plant family?
questions.fact: Almonds, peaches and plums belong to the rose family too.
questions.src: treelib.ca Rosaceae: apples, pears, almonds, apricots, peaches, plums, cherries, strawberries; heath family (Ericaceae) = blueberries/cranberries, textbook

blurb: Parades, football and the calendar story of Thanksgiving

questions.q: Who traditionally arrives at the very end of the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade?
questions.fact: The first parade, in 1924, featured live animals borrowed from the Central Park Zoo.
questions.src: americacomesalive.com balloons history: 1924 live animals borrowed from Central Park Zoo; Santa finale textbook

questions.q: Which cartoon cat was among the parade's first giant balloons, in 1927?
questions.fact: The parade began in 1924 under the name Macy's Christmas Parade.
questions.src: americacomesalive.com: balloons debuted 1927, Felix the most famous; began 1924 as Macy's Christmas Parade (other cats created later)

questions.q: In 1928, what did Macy's do with its giant balloons once the parade ended?
questions.fact: Macy's offered a $100 reward to anyone who returned a balloon after it came down.
questions.src: americacomesalive.com: 1928 helium balloons released, $100 reward for return

questions.q: Which city's Thanksgiving parade, started by Gimbels department store in 1920, predates Macy's?
questions.fact: It is considered the oldest Thanksgiving Day parade in the United States.
questions.src: Wikipedia 6abc Dunkin' Thanksgiving Day Parade: began 1920 by Gimbels; oldest in US

questions.q: Which NFL team began its tradition of hosting a Thanksgiving game in 1934?
questions.fact: The Dallas Cowboys started hosting their own Thanksgiving game in 1966.
questions.src: Wikipedia NFL on Thanksgiving Day: Lions began 1934 hosting Bears; Cowboys 1966

questions.q: Green bean casserole was created in 1955 in the test kitchen of which company?
questions.fact: Creator Dorcas Reilly's handwritten recipe card is kept by the National Inventors Hall of Fame.
questions.src: Smithsonian Magazine: Dorcas Reilly, 1955, Campbell's test kitchen; card in National Inventors Hall of Fame archives

questions.q: Butterball's Turkey Talk-Line, a hotline for holiday cooks, first opened in which decade?
questions.fact: In its first season, six home economists answered about 11,000 turkey questions.
questions.src: Butterball Turkey Talk-Line page: started 1981; six home economists, 11,000 questions

questions.q: The Thanksgiving song 'Over the River and Through the Wood' began as an 1844 poem by whom?
questions.fact: Its original title was 'The New-England Boy's Song about Thanksgiving Day.'
questions.src: Wikipedia Over the River and Through the Wood: Lydia Maria Child, 1844, Flowers for Children; original title

questions.q: By law, US Thanksgiving falls on which Thursday of November?
questions.fact: Until 1939 it was traditionally the last Thursday, which in some years meant the fifth.
questions.src: Wikipedia Franksgiving: last Thursday before 1939; fourth Thursday fixed by Congress from 1942

questions.q: Canadian Thanksgiving falls on which day in October?
questions.fact: Canada's Parliament fixed Thanksgiving on that date in 1957.
questions.src: Wikipedia Thanksgiving (Canada): second Monday of October; 'In 1957, Parliament fixed...'

questions.q: Which president's 1863 proclamation set a nationwide day of Thanksgiving?
questions.fact: Before then, Thanksgiving had mainly been a New England custom.
questions.src: Wikipedia Franksgiving (Lincoln 1863); todayifoundout: previously mainly a New England custom

questions.q: Sarah Josepha Hale, who campaigned for a national Thanksgiving, first published which nursery rhyme in 1830?
questions.fact: Hale edited Godey's Lady's Book, one of the most popular magazines of its day, for 40 years.
questions.src: Wikipedia Mary Had a Little Lamb: first published May 24, 1830 in Hale's Poems for Our Children as 'Mary's Lamb'; Roulstone authorship claim exists, so reworded from 'wrote' to 'first published'. Godey's 40 years: todayifoundout

blurb: Candy bars, bakery classics and the stories behind your sweets

questions.q: Which candy bar, named after a Mars family horse, debuted in 1930?
questions.fact: In the UK and Ireland, Snickers was sold under the name Marathon until 1990.
questions.src: Wikipedia Snickers (re-checked): 1930, named after the Mars family's favorite horse; sold as Marathon in UK/Ireland until 1990

questions.q: The two M's in M&M's stand for Forrest Mars and his partner with which last name?
questions.fact: M&M's were first sold in 1941.
questions.src: Wikipedia M&M's: 'The two Ms represent the last names of Forrest E. Mars Sr. and Bruce Murrie'; introduced Sept 10, 1941

questions.q: Walter Diemer's 1928 bubble gum, sold as Dubble Bubble, was what color?
questions.fact: Pink was reportedly the only food coloring in the factory, and it became the classic bubble gum color.
questions.src: Wikipedia Walter Diemer: 1928, sold as Dubble Bubble; 'pink because it was the only food coloring in the factory'

questions.q: Before a 1985 rename, Sour Patch Kids were sold under what name?
questions.fact: The new name played off the Cabbage Patch Kids craze of the mid-1980s.
questions.src: Mental Floss '9 sweet facts' + AdWeek 'Design Evolution: Sour Patch Kids': originally Mars Men; renamed 1985 for US launch, inspired by Cabbage Patch Kids. 'In Canada' dropped: sources disagree on where Jaret International was based

questions.q: Tiramisu, made with ladyfingers and mascarpone, comes from which country?
questions.fact: Its name means 'pick me up' in Italian.
questions.src: Wikipedia Tiramisu: originated in northeastern Italy; from tirami su, 'pick me up' or 'cheer me up'

questions.q: The Cronut, a croissant-doughnut hybrid, drew long lines in 2013 in which city?
questions.fact: Pastry chef Dominique Ansel filed to trademark the name within nine days of its debut.
questions.src: Wikipedia Cronut: introduced May 10, 2013 at Dominique Ansel Bakery, SoHo, NYC; lines of 100+ by day three; trademark filed within nine days

questions.q: Baked Alaska is ice cream and cake covered in what, then quickly browned?
questions.fact: Air trapped in the meringue insulates the ice cream during its quick trip into a hot oven.
questions.src: COMSOL blog 'Why doesn't the ice cream in a baked Alaska melt?': trapped air in the meringue foam insulates; brief bake in a very hot oven

questions.q: The fruit-topped dessert pavlova is named after Anna Pavlova, a famous Russian what?
questions.fact: Australia and New Zealand have long debated which country created it.
questions.src: Wikipedia Pavlova: named after the Russian ballerina Anna Pavlova; long-standing AU/NZ dispute over origin

questions.q: Chocolate is made from the seeds of which tree?
questions.fact: Cacao pods grow straight out of the tree's trunk and thick branches.
questions.src: growables.org cocoa: 'flowers and fruits on the older branches and trunk (cauliflorous flowering)'; seeds processed to make chocolate

questions.q: Vanilla comes from the seed pods of which type of plant?
questions.fact: The vanilla orchid is native to the tropical Americas, from Mexico to northern Brazil.
questions.src: Britannica vanilla: climbing orchids (Orchidaceae), pods; Wikipedia Vanilla planifolia: native to Mexico, Central America, Colombia and northern Brazil

questions.q: Ruth Wakefield created the chocolate chip cookie in the 1930s at the Toll House Inn in which state?
questions.fact: Nestle later printed her recipe on its chocolate packaging.
questions.src: Lemelson-MIT 'Ruth Wakefield': Toll House on the outskirts of Whitman, Massachusetts, 1930s; Nestle allowed to print the recipe on its packaging

questions.q: Cotton candy was a hit at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair under what name?
questions.fact: Dentist William Morrison and candy maker John C. Wharton invented the machine-spun treat in 1897.
questions.src: Wikipedia Cotton candy: machine-spun cotton candy invented 1897 by dentist William Morrison and confectioner John C. Wharton; introduced at 1904 World's Fair as Fairy Floss. 'Spun Sugar' distractor removed (cotton candy literally is spun sugar)

blurb: Festivals of light, winter customs and celebrations around the globe

questions.q: Diwali, celebrated by millions in India and around the world, is known as the festival of what?
questions.fact: Families light rows of small clay oil lamps called diyas.
questions.src: Britannica 'diya': at Diwali, diyas lit and placed in rows along temples and houses; festival of lights textbook

questions.q: Hanukkah is celebrated for how many nights?
questions.fact: A Hanukkah menorah holds nine candles: one for each night plus a helper candle, the shamash.
questions.src: Wikipedia Hanukkah menorah: nine-branched, eight lights for the eight nights plus the shamash ('helper') used to light them

questions.q: On St. Lucia's Day in Sweden, the girl chosen to play Lucia wears a crown of what?
questions.fact: St. Lucia's Day falls on December 13 and is often marked with saffron buns.
questions.src: Smithsonian 'Lussekatter and Cuccia for St. Lucy's Day': Dec 13; girls wear a crown of candles; saffron buns

questions.q: Loy Krathong, when people float candlelit baskets on rivers, is a famous festival of which country?
questions.fact: A krathong is traditionally a slice of banana tree trunk, decorated with folded banana leaves.
questions.src: Wikipedia Loy Krathong: Thai festival; krathong traditionally a slice of banana tree trunk decorated with folded banana leaves, incense, candle (old fact said made from banana leaves - corrected)

questions.q: Kwanzaa, first celebrated in 1966, begins on December 26 and lasts how many days?
questions.fact: Each day honors one of seven principles, such as unity and creativity.
questions.src: Mental Floss Kwanzaa facts: created 1966 by Maulana Karenga; Dec 26-Jan 1; seven principles incl. Umoja (unity), Kuumba (creativity)

questions.q: Las Posadas processions in Mexico re-enact a search for what?
questions.fact: Las Posadas is celebrated over nine nights, from December 16 to 24.
questions.src: Britannica Kids 'Las Posadas': re-enacts Joseph and Mary's search for lodging; nine nights, Dec 16-24; posada = inn

questions.q: Thanks to a 1974 ad campaign, many families in Japan celebrate Christmas by eating what?
questions.fact: Many families in Japan order their Christmas chicken weeks in advance.
questions.src: Time Out Tokyo 'KFC and Christmas in Japan': national campaign 1974 ('Kentucky is Christmas!'); Christmas orders taken from early November

questions.q: In Italy, which old woman traditionally brings children gifts on the night of January 5?
questions.fact: By tradition, she leaves sweets for good children and lumps of coal for naughty ones.
questions.src: Wikipedia Befana: old woman who delivers gifts on Epiphany Eve (night of Jan 5); sweets for good children, 'coal' for naughty. 'Kindly' dropped (usually depicted as witch-like)

questions.q: During Lunar New Year, the red envelopes given to children traditionally hold what?
questions.fact: In Mandarin Chinese, the red envelopes are called hongbao.
questions.src: Wikipedia Red envelope: contain cash; given at Chinese New Year, mostly to children; Mandarin hongbao

questions.q: During Japan's spring custom of hanami, people gather outdoors to admire what?
questions.fact: Hanami means 'flower viewing' in Japanese.
questions.src: Wikipedia Hanami: 'flower viewing'; almost always cherry blossoms (less often plum)

questions.q: Which round pastry is the signature treat of the Mid-Autumn Festival?
questions.fact: The festival falls on the 15th day of the eighth lunar month, when the moon is full.
questions.src: Wikipedia Mid-Autumn Festival: 15th day of the 8th lunisolar month, night of a full moon; mooncakes eaten

questions.q: Nowruz, the Persian New Year, begins on which day of the year?
questions.fact: Nowruz means 'new day' in Persian.
questions.src: Wikipedia Nowruz: now 'new' + ruz 'day'; day set by the March (spring) equinox

blurb: A grab bag of food science, snack history and surprising origins

questions.q: Which of these 'nuts' is actually a legume, like peas and beans?
questions.fact: Peanut flowers bloom above ground, but the pods grow and ripen underground.
questions.src: Wayne's Word peanut page: peanut is a legume (Fabaceae); flowers above ground, pegs grow into soil, pods complete growth underground

questions.q: Which compound gives chili peppers their heat?
questions.fact: Pharmacist Wilbur Scoville created his scale for rating pepper heat in 1912.
questions.src: Wikipedia Wilbur Scoville: American pharmacist, devised test and scale in 1912 at Parke-Davis; piperine/allicin textbook

questions.q: Quinoa is often called a grain, but botanically it's related to which leafy green?
questions.fact: The United Nations named 2013 the International Year of Quinoa.
questions.src: Wikipedia Quinoa: pseudocereal, amaranth family, related to spinach and amaranth; UN 2013 year

questions.q: In cooking, the Maillard reaction is responsible for what?
questions.fact: It's named for French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard, who described it in 1912.
questions.src: Wikipedia Maillard reaction: named after French chemist Louis Camille Maillard, who first described it in 1912

questions.q: Which chip brand is known for its curved saddle shape and stackable tube?
questions.fact: That saddle shape is a geometric form called a hyperbolic paraboloid.
questions.src: abakcus.com 'Geometry behind Pringles': 'A Pringle is a hyperbolic paraboloid', a saddle surface; tube textbook

questions.q: Momofuku Ando invented instant noodles in 1958 in which country?
questions.fact: His company, Nissin, followed up with Cup Noodles in 1971.
questions.src: NBC News obituary of Momofuku Ando: Chicken Ramen 1958, Cup Noodle 1971, founded Nissin

questions.q: The Oreo cookie debuted in 1912 from which company?
questions.fact: A similar cookie, Sunshine's Hydrox, actually came first, in 1908.
questions.src: The Hustle 'disappearing Hydrox cookies': Sunshine (Loose-Wiles) created Hydrox in 1908; Nabisco shipped first Oreos March 1912

questions.q: Before World War II, Twinkies were filled with cream flavored like which fruit?
questions.fact: Bananas were rationed during World War II, so the filling switched to vanilla cream.
questions.src: Wikipedia Twinkie: Jimmy Dewar, 1930, Continental Baking; banana cream filling; bananas rationed in WWII, switched to vanilla. Old fact's 'still uses' removed

questions.q: The cheesesteak sandwich is a signature food of which US city?
questions.fact: In Philadelphia, the most common cheeses on it are American, provolone and Cheez Whiz.
questions.src: Wikipedia Cheesesteak: Philadelphia; 'American cheese, provolone, and Cheez Whiz are the most commonly used cheeses'. Old fact (Olivieri brothers) dropped: article says the origin story is debated

questions.q: Nachos were invented in 1943 by Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya in which country?
questions.fact: He served them to American visitors in Piedras Negras, just across the border from Eagle Pass, Texas.
questions.src: Wikipedia Nachos (re-checked): Ignacio 'Nacho' Anaya, 1943, Victory Club, Piedras Negras, Coahuila; officers' wives from Fort Duncan (Eagle Pass, TX)

questions.q: The Waldorf salad of apples, celery and mayonnaise was created in the 1890s in which city?
questions.fact: Oscar Tschirky's 1896 cookbook recipe had no nuts; walnuts were added in later versions.
questions.src: barrypopik.com 'Waldorf Salad': created at NYC's Waldorf Hotel 1893-1896, in print 1894; Tschirky's 1896 cookbook recipe = apples, celery, mayonnaise, no nuts; walnuts by 1897

questions.q: Arabica coffee plants are native to the highlands of which country?
questions.fact: Yemen and Ethiopia were likely among the first places to grow coffee as a crop.
questions.src: Wikipedia Coffea arabica: endemic to SW highlands of Ethiopia; Yemen and S. Ethiopia pioneering cultivation regions (Yemen kept out of options)

blurb: Ball drops, lucky foods and midnight traditions around the world

questions.q: Where does New York City's famous New Year's Eve ball drop take place?
questions.fact: The idea came from time balls, which harbors once dropped at a set hour so ships could check their clocks.
questions.src: CNN Style ball design history: ball based on time balls, 19th-century nautical devices for setting ship chronometers; Wikipedia Times Square: first ball Dec 31, 1907

questions.q: Times Square takes its name from which newspaper, which once had its headquarters there?
questions.fact: Before 1904, the area was known as Longacre Square.
questions.src: Britannica Times Square: named for the New York Times in 1904; Wikipedia: formerly Longacre Square, renamed April 8, 1904; Herald Square named for the Herald

questions.q: Which TV host became Dick Clark's co-host on 'New Year's Rockin' Eve' in 2005?
questions.fact: The show first aired on NBC in 1972, hosted by the band Three Dog Night.
questions.src: MediaVillage/HISTORY 'A New Tradition is Born': first aired Dec 31, 1972 on NBC, hosted by Three Dog Night; 'Starting in 2005, Ryan Seacrest joined as cohost'. Wikipedia NYRE confirms; Daly/Fallon/Cooper never hosted it. Reworded to a fixed historical event (no 'lead host')

questions.q: To welcome the year 2000, Times Square debuted a new ball covered in panels of what?
questions.fact: The first ball, in 1907, was made of iron and wood and lit by 100 light bulbs.
questions.src: NPR 'An Abridged Design History of the Ball': 1907 ball of wood, iron and 100 light bulbs; millennium ball covered in Waterford Crystal triangles; CNN confirms Waterford for 2000

questions.q: In Spain, people eat 12 of what at midnight, one for each chime of the clock?
questions.fact: They're called las doce uvas de la suerte, the twelve grapes of luck.
questions.src: Wikipedia Twelve Grapes: las doce uvas (de la suerte), one grape per midnight bell strike

questions.q: On New Year's Eve, the Dutch snack on oliebollen. What are they?
questions.fact: The name oliebollen translates literally as 'oil balls.'
questions.src: Wikipedia Oliebol: Dutch doughnut-like fried dough traditionally eaten on New Year's Eve; oliebollen literally 'oil spheres'

questions.q: In Scotland's Hogmanay tradition, being the first visitor through the door after midnight is called what?
questions.fact: First-footers traditionally bring small gifts, such as coal or shortbread.
questions.src: Wikipedia First-foot: first visitor after midnight; gifts incl. coal, shortbread or black bun, salt. 'Guising' distractor swapped for 'Carolling' (Guising is the answer key in the Halloween Heist deck)

questions.q: On New Year's Eve, Buddhist temples in Japan traditionally ring their bells how many times?
questions.fact: The bell-ringing ceremony is called joya no kane.
questions.src: Wikipedia Joya no Kane: Japanese Buddhist New Year's Eve event; most temples ring the bell 108 times

questions.q: Eating black-eyed peas on New Year's Day is a tradition most associated with which US region?
questions.fact: They're often cooked with rice in a dish called Hoppin' John.
questions.src: Old Farmer's Almanac 'Hoppin' John': black-eyed peas and rice, eaten in the southern US on New Year's Day for luck

questions.q: On New Year's Day, people taking part in a 'polar bear plunge' do what?
questions.fact: In the Netherlands, thousands start the year with a New Year's dip in the North Sea at Scheveningen.
questions.src: IamExpat 'New Year's Dive': Jan 1 North Sea dip, biggest at Scheveningen with some 10,000 people

questions.q: Which Scottish poet wrote down 'Auld Lang Syne' in 1788?
questions.fact: Burns built it on an older Scots folk song; the title means roughly 'old long since.'
questions.src: Wikipedia Auld Lang Syne: Burns wrote it and sent it to the Scots Musical Museum in 1788; based on an older Scottish folk song; title = 'old long since'

questions.q: Greek families cut a New Year's cake called vasilopita. What is hidden inside?
questions.fact: The cake is linked to Saint Basil, whose feast day falls on January 1.
questions.src: Wikipedia Vasilopita: hidden coin or trinket; associated with Saint Basil's day, 1 January. 'A ring' distractor swapped for 'A pea' (a ring could count as a trinket)
